If you use the advanced search page, check the box in the bottom right
corner to "Display search URL for future use".  Depending on the fields you
select, that should give you something like...

http://plants.usda.gov/java/AdvancedSearchServlet?sciname=Astragalus%20miser&dsp_symbol=on&dsp_statefips=on&dsp_family=on&dsp_dur=on&dsp_grwhabt=on&dsp_nativestatuscode=on&dsp_fed_te_status=on&Synonyms=all&viewby=sciname

Just take that URL and paste the species at the end and then use the
readHTMLTable function in the XML package.

url <-
"http://plants.usda.gov/java/AdvancedSearchServlet?dsp_symbol=on&dsp_statefips=on&dsp_family=on&dsp_dur=on&dsp_grwhabt=on&dsp_nativestatuscode=on&dsp_fed_te_status=on&Synonyms=all&viewby=sciname&sciname="

species <- "Astragalus miser"
url2 <- paste(url, species, sep="")
x<-readHTMLTable(url2)

These pages have lots of formatting tables, so the results are quite
messy... Sometimes it helps to count the number of rows in each table, 

sapply(x, nrow)
NULL NULL NULL NULL NULL NULL NULL NULL NULL NULL 
  65    1   56   46   43    9    1    1    1    1 

But once you find the table you need (#8), then you can just select that
directly.

x[[8]]

or use the which option to get table 8.  I also removed the newlines from
column names...
x2<-readHTMLTable(url2, which=8, stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
names(x2) <- gsub("(.*?)\r\n.*", "\\1", names(x2) )

messages.subject: [R-sig-eco] Fwd: log transformed response GLM versus LM
messages.subject_clean: log transformed response GLM versus LM
messages.body_plain:
Dear Drew and Liz,

Thank you both very much for your help in explaining this to me. I was
pleasantly surprised to have found your answers in my mailbox after having
thought that I made a mistake in posting a question right before many go on
vacation! I'm happy that you found this to be an interesting example. You
have indeed helped me better understand the realm of GLMs.

I believe that I have made one error in my description of the problem -
that my concentrations (Y) may not actually have increasing measurement
error with concentration. My confusion comes from the fact that the error
of estimated chlorophyll via remote sensing algorithms is often given as a
percent (e.g. 50%). This relationship is usually derived via a log
concentration plot of in situ versus predicted values, where the error is
pretty much normally distributed when observed on this log-scale (see the
Globcolour validation report Appendices for an example:
http://www.globcolour.info/validation/report/GlobCOLOUR_FVR_v1.1.pdf). So
this is different in that the error of the model's prediction is plotted
versus an independent data set.

So, I believe for the reasons you mention, I will stick with the log-link
GLM, but rather assume a Gaussian distribution for my in situ estimated
(Y). This solves the problem of predicting negative values and actually
gives a better fit over that of the LM.

I unfortunately do not have a large data set for my model (nor an
independent data set for validation), so I am planning to present the
confidence intervals around my predicted values. Interestingly, this is not
out of line with the expectation that predictions of higher concentrations
have larger confidence intervals, and thus, if an independent data set were
available, the predicted vs in situ plot might closely resemble the more
typical remote sensing validation plots.

pred <- predict(GAUSS.LOG.GLM, type="response", se.fit=TRUE)

LIM <- range(c(pred$fit-(pred$se.fit*1.96), pred$fit+(pred$se.fit*1.96),
DF$Y))
plot(pred$fit ~ DF$Y, t="n", xlim=LIM, ylim=LIM)
abline(0,1,lty=1, col=8, lwd=2)
segments(x0=DF$Y, x1=DF$Y, y0=pred$fit-(pred$se.fit*1.96),
y1=pred$fit+(pred$se.fit*1.96), lwd=2)
points(pred$fit ~ DF$Y, pch=1, lwd=2)


Again thanks for your help,
Marc




On Wed, Dec 26, 2012 at 1:55 PM, Liz Pryde <elizabethpryde at gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Marc,
>
> The main difference between the 2 methods is that with linear models (lm)
> you are trying to shape the data to fit the model's assumptions. In GLMs
> you're trying to fit a model to the data. The family you choose in order to
> estimate the error distribution of your data (account for the mean-variance
> relationship, in your case the increasing variance with mean). The link
> aims to linearise the relationship between your predictor(s) and your
> response variable. You can usually decide what this is by looking at the
> distribution of the data and the way it was collected. What is 'better'
> about the GLM is that it gives reasonable results (ie non-negative where
> negative values are impossible) because it captures the error structure
> better leading to more accurate predictions.
>
> Of course, large amounts of zeroes are hard to model, but there are a
> number of ways around this - using negative binomial distribution,
> zero-inflated models, or positive distributions with a mass at zero (e.g.
> tweedie). With GLMs and their extensions you have more flexibility for such
> options.
>
> Really, the best way to check is to do your model diagnostics. Which
> approach gives less or no pattern to the residuals? That approach should be
> your answer.
>
> A good paper on the topic is Bob O'Hara's: "do not log transform count
> data" in Methods in Ecology & Evolution.
> You can get it here:
> http://www.mendeley.com/profiles/bob-ohara/
>
> Hope that helps,
> Liz
>
> On 26/12/2012, at 4:35 PM, Drew Tyre <atyre2 at unl.edu> wrote:
>
> I can see why this would be frustrating - you come to different
> conclusions about X2 depending on which model you fit.
>
> Using a GLM with a log link and Gaussian observation distribution is
> not the same as using lm on log transformed data. In both cases the
> observations are assumed to be normally distributed with constant
> variance; this implies that the observations can come from -infinity
> to +infinity. In the log link glm however, the expected value of y is
> constrained to be larger than zero. That is, even though the
> observations y can be less than zero, the expected value of the y is
> strictly greater than zero because of the log link.
>
> In contrast, log transforming the y maps the domain [0,infinity) into
> (-infinity, infinity), which is exactly what is required for the
> validity of the assumed normal distribution of the errors. Thus the
> distribution of the observations on the original scale is log-normal,
> and all is well.
>
> The test of this idea is to see if a glm with log-link is allowed to
> have values of y <0:
> # Try a parametric bootstrap to see what the assumed models really look
> like
> mu <- fitted(GAUSS.LOG.GLM)
>
> # the dispersion parameter is the residual variance, roughly.
> disp = summary(GAUSS.LOG.GLM)$dispersion
> # and this generates negative numbers
> y.test <- rnorm(length(mu),mu,varfunc(mu)*sqrt(disp))
> # but you can still fit a log-link glm, as long as you provide starting
> values
> glm(y.test~X1+X2,data=DF,start=c(-5,12,-8),family=gaussian(link="log"))
>
> However, even if that explains why you get radically different
> answers, it doesn't really help you decide which one is better! The
> log(Y) lm and the Gamma glm are making the correct assumptions about
> the distribution of Y, that is, that Y > 0, and that var(Y) ~ Y. From
> a pure "prediction" perspective the Gaussian glm is doing better by
> making incorrect assumptions, but that extra performance is focused
> entirely on those few very large values. One way to see this is to
> look at plots of the residuals
>
> par(mfrow=c(2,2))
> plot(LOG.LM)
> plot(GAUSS.LOG.GLM)
>
> In the first plot, you can see that the residuals are pretty well
> distributed, and there is no heteroscedasticity. In the 2nd plot, the
> heteroscedasticity (dependence of var(Y) on Y) is clear in the
> scale-location plot, and you can see the strong effect of the large
> observations in the plot of residuals vs. leverage (points 15 and 25
> have cooks distance > 1) and are the 2 largest observations in the
> dataset. You mentioned that the measurement error increases with
> concentration - that suggests that these large points *should* be
> downweighted with respect to smaller observations - they are less
> accurate. This is happening naturally in models that allow for
> increasing variance with increasing Y (log-normal and gamma)
>
> I would go with the Gamma GLM, I think. The error distribution meets
> the assumptions, the residuals look ok, and the prediction performance
> is better than the LOG.LM.
>
> Thanks for posting an interesting example.
>
> hth
>
> On Dec 22, 2012, at 5:53 AM, Marc Taylor <marchtaylor at gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear r-sig-ecology group,
>
>
> I am having some difficulties understanding the difference between results
>
> obtained for a multiple regression linear model fit either by a General
>
> Linear Model (LM) or a Generalized Linear Model (GLM).
>
>
> I have attached an example data set in which I am trying to fit Y ~ X1 +
>
> X2. Y is a concentration and the distribution of observed values is highly
>
> skewed towards zero (with no negative numbers). I would expect that the
>
> error in measuring Y increases with it's value. An analog would be in the
>
> estimation of Chla concentrations via remote sensing - e.g. the typical
>
> error of a SeaWifs estimate is usually given as a percent of the
>
> concentration so that large values have wider confidence intervals
>
> surrounding them.
>
>
> I originally started out fitting a multiple LM to the data without
>
> log-transforming Y. This is probably incorrect given that Y is so skewed
>
> toward zero, and that model can predict negative Y values (which is not
>
> possible). Now, I am hoping to fit a model to the log-transformed Y, but
>

messages.subject: [R-sig-eco] Global overlap index
messages.body_plain:
Dear Listers,

I measured pollen grains (variable POLLEN_SIZE) of anthers from three
levels from the same species (variable ANTHER) in many populations
(variable POP). I am most interested in pollen size overlapping among the
three levels among populations. The number of measures per level and per
population varies from 2 - 60 individuals, due the number of flowers
available in each population.

I tried to use some Mixed Models to analyze my data, but it seems to be
over parameterized, besides unbalanced (and I don’t know how to handle with
it!). I believe that reducing the pollen size per population in a global
overlapping index could be a good way to use it as response variable in
models.

I have searched for overlapping index, but I could not find any global
index for my case. I have only found some pairwise overlapping index.

So, my questions are, 1) Is it possible to use some global overlapping
index to quantify how much overlapped are the anther levels in each
population? 2) Does anyone know if there is any function developed to r to
my case?

Any suggestions are welcome.

Best wishes

Nicolay

Greetings all -

I'm in the process of fitting some population models and had a question
regarding the simulation process in R.  Below I've pasted a simple code for
logistic growth with some stochasticity in the growth rate parameter ("r" -
see the runif part of the code).  If you run continue to repeat this code
you get a similar, but distinct and unique population model (i.e., graph of
population versus time) each time.  What I'm figure out is how to automate
the process to do this say...10 times...and plot all ten simulations on one
graph.  I'm trying to use a matrix approach, and fill each element.
However, I'm having difficulties figuring things out.

I appreciate any assistance offered,

Peter


Code:


test.logistic<-function(alpha=0.01, r0=1.2, f=0.2, N0=80, t=100) {
r<-c(r0, numeric(t))
for (i in 1:t) r[i+1]<- {
runif(1,0.8,1.1)
}
N<-c(N0, numeric(t))
for (k in 1:t) N[k+1]<- {
(N[k]+r[i]*N[k]*(1-(N[k]*alpha))-f*N[k])
}
return(N)
}
Nts<-bevholt()
t<-100
plot(0:t, Nts, type="l")

construct a data.frame, where each row represents a unique scenario and

   xx <- matrix(0, nrow = length(t), ncol = length(x0))
   xx[1, ] <- x0
   for (i in t)  x0 <- xx[i, ] <- x0 + r * x0 * (1 - x0)
   xx
}

adonis() and db-RDA (capscale) are indeed very similar, but they differ in handling negative distances due to negative eigenvalues and complex eigenvectors. Briefly, adonis() handles them but capscale() does not. Otherwise the results are very similar. If you do not need a graphical presentation, I recommend you use adonis().

> ) Anyway I am mainly interested to 
> understand the difference between analyses based on distance matrix of the environemental gradient (Mantel test), or on the gradient directly. 

So would I. I'm working to improve my understanding, but this is a tricky issue. However, in *most* (but perhaps not in all) cases it is better to work via gradients directly, and via rectangular data instead of distances/dissimilarities. Method working with rectangular data and gradients in vegan include capscale(), adonis() and betadisper(). Methods that work with dissimilarities in vegan include mantel(), mantel.partial(), anosim(), bioenv(), mrpp() and meandist(). The former set is usually preferred.

Cheers, Jari Oksanen

messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 2013-01-15 at 14:40 +0000, Emmanuel Castella wrote:
> Dear R-users
> I am trying to understand the difference between the GCV score
> returned by summary() of a gam object in the mgcv package, and the
> output of a k-fold cross-validation of the same gam model. Thank you
> in advance for any answer or reference to a published document.
> Sincerely
> Emmanuel Castella

I don't have all the details to hand, but as no one has replied,
publicly at least, I'll have a stab. GCV is a means of approximating the
results of an explicit CV. The GCV score in mgcv:::gam() is the minimum
GCV score arrived at during fitting for various value of smoothness
penalty; in other words it is the thing that was minimised to arrive at
the fitted model for which smoothness selection was performed.

If you did a k-fold CV to find the optimal smoothing parameters, the
degrees of freedom for the fitted smooth(s) should be similar to the
degrees of freedom used by the model when GCV was used.

The difference between the two is that GCV approximates what you'd get
if you did the actual CV without having to actually fit all those models
during the CV steps. Not doing all the fitting can be a huge
computational saving!

For the details I strongly suggest you read Simon Wood's book

  Wood, S.N. (2006) Generalized Additive Models: An
  Introduction with R. Chapman and Hall/CRC.

And having said all that, Simon and colleagues have shown that GCV can
under-smooth data, especially when the objective function is very flat
in the region of the optimal model. The conclusion that I draw from
their papers is that using `method = "REML"` or `method = "ML"` is
usually provides the best-performing smoothness selection and in
addition one can turn on extra penalties (one via `select = TRUE`, the
other via an argument to each `s()` term) that will perform model
selection (i.e. shrink terms out of the model) for you.

HTH

G

We have had this problem sometimes in svd in vegan functions (rda, cca), and then LINPACK = TRUE has helped. However, this is not a good solution as LINPACK is phasing out from R. In the current development version (and probably in the next R release later this year), LINPACK is defunct, and this solution won't work. 

It seems that the basic problem  is in the svd function of the LAPACK that is used as the default now and that will be the only choice later this year. LAPACK is an external library that is beyond the control of package developers and R core team so that these problems may be unsolvable. It seems that the problems with the LAPACK code are so common that even the help page of svd() function tells about them:

     Unsuccessful results from the underlying LAPACK code will result
     in an error giving a positive error code (most often ?1?): these
     can only be interpreted by detailed study of the FORTRAN code but
     mean that the algorithm failed to converge.

Sometimes rescaling of the data (= multiplying with a suitable constant) has helped, too, and that may be the only thing we can try once LINPACK = TRUE option disappears within a few months.

messages.subject: [R-sig-eco] Standardizing data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Ben Bolker suggested I float this by this group.

After 26 years of living and working the the Neotropics I have moved 
back to the U.S.

One of the first issues for relative abundance of bats from acoustic 
monitoring is how best to standardize data sets for comparison.   It was 
easy in the tropics with a straight forward application of my Acoustic 
Activity Index (AI) [Miller, B. W. 2001. A method for determining 
relative activity of free flying bats using a new activity index for 
acoustic monitoring. Acta Chiropterologica. 3: 93-105].

This uses the occurrence of each species by 1-minute time blocks and is 
then standardized by "Unit Effort"  which is the total sample time each 
night in hours. With a night length that was fairly standard with only a 
small ? of 1 hr or so for seasonal variation and very small 
night-to-night change this seem OK.

However looking at data from here in the northern latitudes, I am 
beginning to think/ponder that I need something else in addition. The 
night length not only changes rapidly night-to-night during the summer, 
but has a very wide ?.  So using my AI -occurrences per each 1-minute 
time interval standardized by sampling time that I used in the tropics 
may not reflect a realistic comparison measure up here in the north?

So my question is how to incorporate the length of each night into the 
AI standardized by sample time?
How best to integrate the night length since that is one of the key 
factors constraining bat activity?

So e.g. a standardized sample time of 8 hours with an AI may be high, 
but during some times of the summer when  the night is relatively short  
however a similar standardized AI value would not be directly comparable 
to seasons with longer nights when activity may be longer as well.

*/R/* seems awesome for running repetitive calculations once one has the 
code line script.  So I am trying to see how to develop such a new 
standardized /R/ code for a DF with the simple AI values that have 
already been standardized by unit effort that include the ever changing 
sunset-sunrise data (that readily available and/or generated by altitude 
for the sampling site) to use the night length in a way to further 
adjust the data?

A suggestion on generating the sunset-sunrise then calculating the night 
length for each night then using that value to further adjust the 
"standardized AI value" is what I am trying to figure out.  The 
standardized AI is already coded into a master database as an output so 
that is readily available by species and location.

For working out GGplot temporal activity plots by minute for each night 
it took bit of hand holding by Hadley as R does not (or at lead did not) 
"do time well".  Not sure what can be done with this idea.  The 
crossover midnight may not be an issue for this calculation since we 
just need a total night length in decimal hours.

Moon phase and % illumination is yet another issue, but not relevant at 
the moment.:-)


Examples of what these DF would look like.


Then I need to have a way to generate the night length for each sampling 
night and further adjust data for realistic comparisons of relative 
activity that translates to relative abundance.

Any and all suggestions welcome.  And the bats will depend on it.

Bruce

messages.body_plain:
Dear members

I am very happy to finally be a part of this community. I often come to
this place to find answers for my problems. But this is the first time I
actually post a question myself to the mailing list, so I'm sorry in
advance for any mistakes I make.

My question is about how I can run an adonis test with multiple responses.
In addition I wonder if there is a good solution to empty rows.

But first a bit of background info:
I am a master student in general ecology, and I am testing if three
different forest management categories contain different species
compositions of beetles. In each forest management category, I have put out
window traps for a couple of months, and identified all the species caught.

I will do this test on beetles in general, as well as sub-groups of beetles
(predators, fungivores etc). But the predictor variables will be the same
in every test (namely the forest management category the beetles have been
caught in).

So here is the thing (question 1):
Since adonis, is a multivariate test (at least PERMANOVA is, and the tests
are identical as far as I understand), I figured it should be possible to
use all the different beetle groups as separate responses in one test.
But when I try to run the test, I only get one p-value returned. Instead I
would like separate p-values for each response (that is, each beetle
group).
Is this possible to do? And if so, how  will the significance of one group
affect the others? I have searched trough several forums and books, but I
find no answer to the question.

This is what I tried to do:
I have two groups of beetles, groupA and groupB. They are normal matrixes,
with traps in rows and species in columns, and each box is number of
observations of that beetle in that trap. They contain no other info
(except column and row names).

R code:
Y = cbind(groupA, groupB)
fit = adonis(Y ~ labels, permutations=4999)
fit

This method is inspired by the example given here:
http://127.0.0.1:10773/help/library/stats/help/summary.manova

In the example they get the P-value of every response variable (seemingly
independent of each other).

However, when I try to run this code, I only get one p-value returned.

messages.body_plain:
Keith,

I've posted a similar question before and got no helpful response. I think
that's  because no one has developed a straightforward way to do this in
R. Hope I'm proven wrong. Having said that, I CAN  tell you how to
properly test the within-subjects effects (including time and the time x
treatment interaction, which you said you were interested in). Just
realize that the p-value for the between-subjects treatment effects will
be wrong, because it uses the residual error term to get it. The issue is
that, as far as I know, no one has developed code to enable you to use two
different error terms in adonis. Again, I hope someone proves me wrong.

Try this code.

First, you need to define a variable that represents the observation upon
which you're taking repeated observations, I.e., the "subject." In your
case, these would be your "plots." The plots should be nested within the
treatments.

adonis(nema.troph.bc~Treatment*Time + plot,data=nema,strata=plot)


Strata treats your plots like blocks. Again, note that you can only
interpret the p-values for the within-subjects effects (time,
treatment*time). The p-value will be wrong for the treatment effect.
Unfortunately, you cannot solve this problem by simply averaging the
responses among years within plots and then running a separate analysis to
determine between-subjects treatment effects because the analysis uses
pairwise distances, rather than distance from a centroid. When you use
bray-curtis distance, the average of responses among years is not the
centroid.

Hope this helps.

Good luck,

Steve

Pedro,
I don't know why it's limiting your axes, but I see a couple of issues with
your analysis.

1. If you only have 9 samples you don't want to use 9 predictor variables.
My multivariate mentors try to stick to a minimum of 3 samples per
predictor included in the model.  I'm not sure where this rule of thumb
comes from, but it's worked pretty well for me.  I think McCune & Grace
(2002) recommend about 5 (If I recall correctly.  I don't have the book in
front of me).  More is always better.

2. If you are running a CCA, you shouldn't need to do the Hellinger
transform.  Log or square-root might reduce the skew if that is an issue,
but my understanding is that the Hellinger transform is used to linearize
the response data so that you can run an RDA on community data.  It has
advantages, such as a meaningful adjusted R^2, but you may still find
reviewers that balk at RDAs on community data.

If you find an alternative analysis method, I'd be interested in hearing
about it.  I have a similar dataset that I am dealing with.

Best,
Jesse

Hello,

I was wondering if this approach is reasonable and I would be happy about
any comments.
For testing differences between treatments (Control, Impact) in the BACI
that Keith described I thought to use pairwise before-after dissimilarities
as below:

library(vegan)

# some data
d <- matrix(round(rnorm(16*6, 1, 0.25), 1), 16, 6, dimnames = list(1:16,
paste0("SP", 1:6)))

# the BACI-design, C = "control", "I" = "impact"
m <- expand.grid(1:4, Treatment = c("C", "I"), BA = c("before",
"after"))[-1]
m$matchID <- c(rep(1:8, 2))
(m <- data.frame(m[, 3:1], row.names = NULL))

# data with equally abundant species across all groups:
cbind(m, d)

# simulate effect only for BA-level "after" in treatment-group "I":
ran <- function() round(rnorm(16, c(rep(1, 12), rep(2, 4)), 0.25), 1)

# apply ran() to some of the species
for(i in c(1,3,6)) d[, i] <- ran()

# see data with simulated effect for species 1, 3 & 6 at BA-level "after"
# and treatment-level "I":
cbind(m, d)

# check the effect in an ordination diagramm
# you'll see that in the control-group "after" is
# similar to control "before" and similar to the impact-group "before"
# whereas in the impact-group 'after' is very dissimilar and thus
# exhibits a location-shift:
sol <- metaMDS(d, "bray")

plot(sol,type="n")
ordipointlabel(sol, display = "sites", pch ="")
points(sol, display = "sites", select=which(m$BA=="before"),
       pch = 21, col="black", bg="black")
points(sol, display = "sites", select=which(m$BA=="after"),
       pch = 21, col="black", bg="white")
ordihull(sol, group=paste0(m$T, m$BA), lty=2)

# Now, what if I don't test a shift in locations, as I would with adonis -
# I could rather simplify the hypothesis to: "In the impact-group the
'after' plots will be
# more dissimilar from the 'before' plots compared to the control-plots".
To test this I could take the
# the pairwise "before-after" dissimilarities and use this as a new
variable in
# any one-way test for univariate data, like so:

# pairwise (before-after) dissimilarities:
dis_pws <- data.frame(Dissim = do.call("cbind", list(by(d, m$matchID,
function(x) vegdist(x[1:2,], "bray")))))
dis_pws$Treatment <-  gl(2, 4, labels = c("Control", "Impact"))

summary(lm(Dissim ~ Treatment, dis_pws))
dev.new()
boxplot(Dissim ~ Treatment, dis_pws, ylab = "Before-After Dissimlarity")

messages.subject_clean: cocorresp to determine best of several predictor communities
messages.body_plain:
Dear List Members,

I am using the 'cocorresp' package and trying to compare several pairs of
communities. My goal would be to see which of several communities best
predicts a final community. Say, for instance, that I have four communities
A, B, C and D. I want to know which community best predicts D. To further
complicate things, I have more data points for some communities than
others. For instance communities A and B and D have 100 sites associated
with them, while C only was measured at 75 sites (lets imagine it wasn't
measured in the last 25 sites). So I run

A.pred <- coca(x =A, y = D, method = “pred”, reg.method = “eigen” n.axes =
10)
B.pred <- coca(x =B, y = D, method = “pred”, reg.method = “eigen” n.axes =
10)
C.pred <- coca(x =C, y = D[1:75,], method = “pred”, reg.method = “eigen”
n.axes = 10)

I then apply crossvalidation, as in (Braak & Schaffers 2004).

A.crossval <- crossval(x = A.pred, n.axes = 10)
A.cvax <- which.max(A.crossval$CVfit)
A.cvmax <- max(A.crossval$CVfit)

B.crossval <- crossval(x = B.pred, n.axes = 10)
B.cvax <- which.max(B.crossval$CVfit)
B.cvmax <- max(B.crossval$CVfit)

C.crossval <- crossval(x = C.pred, n.axes = 10)
C.cvax <- which.max(C.crossval$CVfit)
C.cvmax <- max(C.crossval$CVfit)

Thus X.cvax is the number of axes that give the best crossvalidation score
for community X predicting community D. X.cvax max is that best
crossvalidation score.  I think that if X.cvmax is positive, that suggests
that the model can predict come fraction of the structure of community D
from community X (where X is the community (A, B or C) in question) (as
suggested in Schaffers et al 2008).

Now, I want to know whether A, B or C best predicts D. Because C is only 75
data points, I expect A.cvmax and B.cvmax should be inflated relative to
C.cvmax, so I shouldn't be able to use these values to cross compare
predictive power.

One approach that I think might work is to run permutest to generate
percent fits for each axis that crossvalidation suggests I should include
in the model.

A.perm <- permutest(mo.pred, n.axes = A.cvax)
B.perm <- permutest(mo.pred, n.axes = B.cvax)
C.perm <- permutest(mo.pred, n.axes = C.cvax)

I can then ask what percentage of the community of X predicts what percent
of community Y using the pcent.fit value from the permutest objects. I
think this value is independent of sample size, but am not sure. Does
anybody else know? I could either do this for the first axis, or for the
sum all axes in the model. I'm not sure if the second option is legitimate

Option 1
A.ax1 <- A.perm$pcent.fit[1]
B.ax1 <- B.perm$pcent.fit[1]
C.ax1 <- C.perm$pcent.fit[1]

Option 2
A.all <- sum(A.perm$pcent.fit[1:A.cvax])
B.all <- sum(A.perm$pcent.fit[1:B.cvax])
C.all <- sum(B.perm$pcent.fit[1:C.cvax])

So my first question is, when comparing communities with different but
overlapping sample sizes(all 75 sample sites in C are the same sample sites
as the first 75 in A and B), if

A.all >B.all > C.all

or if A.ax1 > B.ax1 > C.ax1,

can I then say that A is the best predictor community for community D?

More specifically, is this approach a legitimate way of comparing
communities with different sample sizes in which the sample locations
overlap. If not is there a better way of making such a comparison? Perhaps
the co-correspondence method is not appropriate for making this kind of
comparison. I notice that most literature to date uses co-correspondence in
conjunction with cca to determine whether a different community or
environmental parameters best predict a given community. If
co-correspondence is not appropriate, could somebody explain why and
suggest a better method?

References:

 Braak CJF ter, Schaffers AP. (2004). Co-Correspondence Analysis: A New
Ordination Method to Relate Two Community Compositions. Ecology 85:834–846.

Schaffers AP, Raemakers IP, Sýkora KV, Braak CJF ter. (2008). Arthropod
Assemblages Are Best Predicted by Plant Species Composition. Ecology
89:782–794.

 Thanks everyone for your consideration in this matter.

Sincerely,

Jacob Cram

Graduate Student
Department of Biological Sciences
University of Southern California

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Posting this query again as no one replied.

I need to create a way to standardize bat sampling data in northern 
latitudes not only by the Activity Index standardized by sample time 
(unit effort) but by the constantly changing night length.

This was easy in the tropics with a straight forward application of my 
Acoustic Activity Index (AI) [Miller, B. W. 2001. A method for 
determining relative activity of free flying bats using a new activity 
index for acoustic monitoring. Acta Chiropterologica. 3: 93-105].

This uses the occurrence of each species by 1-minute time blocks and is 
then standardized by "Unit Effort"  which is the total sample time each 
night in hours. With a night length that was fairly standard with only a 
small ± of 1 hr or so for seasonal variation and very small 
night-to-night change this seem OK.

However looking at data from here in the northern latitudes,I need 
something else in addition.   The night length not only changes rapidly 
night-to-night during the summer, but has a very wide ±.  So using only 
AI -occurrences per each 1-minute time interval standardized by sampling 
time previously used in the tropics may not reflect a realistic 
comparison measure up here in the north.

So my question is how to incorporate the length of each night into the 
AI standardized by sample time?
How best to integrate the night length since that is one of the key 
factors constraining bat activity?

*/R/* seems awesome for running repetitive calculations once one has the 
code line script.  So I am trying to see how to develop such a new 
standardized /R/ code for two data sets, one a DF with the simple AI 
values that have already been standardized by unit effort and another 
that includes the ever changing sunset-sunrise data.

For working out GGplot temporal activity plots by minute for each night 
it took bit of hand holding by Hadley as R does not (or at lead did not) 
"do time well".  Not sure what can be done with standardizing the data 
with changing night lengths form one night to the.   The crossover 
midnight may not be an issue for this calculation since we just need a 
total night length in decimal hours.

Moon phase and % illumination is yet another issue, but not relevant at 
the moment.:-)

Any and all suggestions welcome and the bats will depend on it.

Bruce

messages.body_plain:
Bruce,

Standardizing might not be the best way to go if you have low counts.
You can possibly assume that events follow a homogeneous Poisson
process and rate varies with night length (linear or quadratic) [Y|x ~
Poisson(phi); log(phi)=f(x)]. You can estimate corresponding
coefficients by glm(). I think controlling for night length
differences work even if you throw in other covariates as additive
effects on the log scale.

You can get sunrise /sunset times from maptools::sunriset, be careful
with timezones though.

Cheers,

Peter

messages.body_plain:
Dear members.

I have a relatively simple question about how to create a formula in
adonis, when I have observations that are spatially clustered, and a block
design.

Here is a simple description of my study design:
I have three forest management categories.
In each management category I have several clusters of logs.
In each cluster, I have selected 5 logs randomly, and mounted an insect
trap on each selected log.
In addition, for one of the 5 logs, I have mounted a smaller, but similar,
type of insect trap.

My question is if there is a significant difference in species composition
between forest management categories. And I would like to include both
types of traps in the same test.

messages.subject: [R-sig-eco] question on gls model interpretation
messages.body_plain:
Dear Iris,

The expected value of any treatment combination can be calculated as sum 
of the coefficients. For example:
E(no comptetitors, no insecticide) = Intercept
E(many competitors, high concentration) =  Intercept + conditionold + 
contaminationhigh + conditionold:contaminationhigh

The non-significant interactions would mean that effects of competition 
and insecticide are simple summed.

You have two interaction parameters that significantly differ from zero. 
For example, conditionold:contaminationhigh=1.2005231. This value can be 
interpreted by two ways. High insecticede concentration has a strong 
negative effect if no competion (contaminationhigh=-1.2825250), but it 
has negligible effect, if competition is stong: 
-1.2825250+1.2005231=-0.0820019. The interaction parameter measures the 
difference between two levels of competition in the effect of insecticide.
Another interpretation is that interaction coefficient measures the 
difference between two levels of insecticide treatment in the effect of 
strong competition (ie. in the decrease of abundance caused by strong 
competition).
 From mathematical point of view these two interpretations are 
equivalent. You can choose either.



Best wishes


Zoltan

glm.nb(Counts ~ Treatment + offset(log(Duration)) + offset(log(CD$PodMigHrPeriodWeight)))



I'm confused by the difference in weights and offsets in glm and glm.nb. Any help would be wonderful.



Chandra
